title: Build, Don't Play: Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players

Title:Build, Don't Play: Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Can LLM agents carry a hard real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against people? We study this in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, an eight-player auto-battler with stochastic shops and battles, hidden information and nearly a thousand interacting cards. We present AutoTavern, a self-improving research system: specialised LLM research agents share a typed research memory, every claim passes verification gates, and live games close the loop, so the agents improve the simulator, opponents and policy and, from the same feedback, their own research process; a human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. In 20 days AutoTavern built TavernGym, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game, and delivered 23 versions of TavernAgent, trained with PPO against opponents calibrated to real games. TavernAgent plays complete games on the live ladder by itself: its rating rose from 6,000 to about 15,000 and, on the public leaderboard's measure, its last 20 records average a placement of 1.60 with 80% first places, better than the server's ten highest-rated players on every statistic (2.34, 59%). TavernBench, 960 tasks in 40 scenarios, shows that the system the agents built is the strongest player: TavernAgent answers 91% of the play tasks against at most 63% for frontier LLMs, and decides in 0.03 s where they need up to 26 s; within the second a live turn allows, it keeps 90% and no LLM more than 26%. LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source TavernBench and TavernGym at this https URL.

report.summary: A self-improving LLM research agent system spent 20 days building a Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI that outperforms the game's ten highest-rated ladder players.
report.background: Games have long served as AI proving grounds, from AlphaGo to OpenAI Five, because they offer clean objectives and measurable skill. Hearthstone Battlegrounds is a harder target: an eight-player auto-battler with randomised shops, hidden information, simultaneous opponents and nearly a thousand interacting cards, played on a roughly one-second decision clock. Meanwhile, the past two years have seen a wave of 'AI scientist' systems that use LLM agents to run experiments, write code and iterate on research questions. What has been missing is evidence that such agents can carry an open-ended, messy, real-world problem all the way from raw data to an artefact that genuinely competes with humans. This paper tests exactly that, and also probes a subtler question: whether LLMs are better at building systems than at being the system.
key_points: AutoTavern's design separates roles: specialised LLM research agents share a typed research memory, every claim must pass verification gates before being trusted, and live game results feed back into the loop. Agents improve the simulator, the opponent pool and the playing policy, and also revise their own research process. A human sets goals and rules on genuinely ambiguous game mechanics.

In 20 days the system produced TavernGym, described as the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game, plus 23 successive versions of TavernAgent trained with PPO against opponents calibrated to real ladder statistics. That is a simulator, a training pipeline and a policy — built largely by LLM agents, not by a human engineering team.

On the live ladder TavernAgent climbed from a 6,000 rating to roughly 15,000. Over its last 20 recorded games it averaged a placement of 1.60 with 80% first places, versus 2.34 and 59% for the server's ten highest-rated human players — better on every reported statistic.

TavernBench, a new 960-task, 40-scenario evaluation, shows where the value lies: TavernAgent answers 91% of play tasks against at most 63% for frontier LLMs, and decides in 0.03 seconds where those models need up to 26 seconds. Under the one-second live turn budget it retains 90% accuracy; no LLM exceeds 26%.

The headline claim is a division of labour: LLM agents 'build far better than they play.' Rather than asking a frontier model to make each in-game decision, the agents wrote the code, trained the network and tuned the opponents, leaving fast, narrow inference to a small PPO policy.
report.impact: The result reframes what LLM agents are for. Instead of treating a frontier model as the runtime decision-maker, the paper positions it as a builder of infrastructure — simulators, training loops, evaluation harnesses — with a small specialised policy doing the fast work. Verified research memory and claim-checking gates offer a practical template for keeping long-running autonomous agents honest, which matters for anyone shipping agentic pipelines. For developers, it suggests that domain simulators are the highest-leverage asset and that latency-critical tasks should be distilled into trained models rather than prompted. For users, it hints at agents that quietly engineer tools in the background. Caveats remain: humans still adjudicated rules, the domain is one game, and sim-to-real fidelity is self-reported.
report.tools: Watch for the promised open-source releases of TavernGym (the full Battlegrounds simulator) and TavernBench (960 tasks across 40 scenarios). To replicate the stack, pair PPO implementations such as CleanRL or Stable-Baselines3 with a multi-agent orchestration framework — LangGraph, AutoGen or CrewAI — and use DSPy for structured, verifiable agent prompts. PettingZoo suits multi-agent environments. For Battlegrounds data and replay analysis, Hearthstone Deck Tracker and Firestone provide community telemetry to calibrate opponents.
